items.prompt:
Read this story below.

I have watched the family across the street for years. Every morning the little girl runs to the mailbox. Every evening the old man sits on the porch. I know things about them they do not know about me.

Who is the narrator? What is unusual or interesting about this narrator?
items.answer: The narrator is an unnamed 'I' who observes the family from across the street. What is interesting is that we do not know who the narrator is, or whether they are a person, an animal, or something else. The last line ('things about them they do not know about me') creates mystery and makes the reader wonder about the narrator's identity.

steps: First-person narration: 'I have watched,' 'I know.' The narrator is anonymous. They observe but are not observed. The phrase 'they do not know about me' raises questions: who or what is this narrator? A neighbor? A tree? A ghost? The narrator's identity is deliberately hidden, which is an interesting authorial choice. First-graders should identify it as first-person and notice the mystery.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

Part 1: Leo walked into the kitchen. He smelled something burning. His dad was at the stove.

Part 2: I was at the stove when Leo walked in. I knew I had burned the eggs. His face said everything.

The narrator changes between Part 1 and Part 2. What changes? Why might an author tell the same scene from two different points of view?
items.answer: In Part 1, a third-person narrator describes the scene from Leo's perspective. In Part 2, a first-person narrator (the dad) tells the same scene from his own point of view. An author might do this to show that two characters experience the same event differently, revealing both sides of a situation.

steps: Part 1: 'Leo walked,' 'He smelled,' 'His dad.' Third-person, follows Leo. Part 2: 'I was at the stove,' 'I knew,' 'I had burned.' First-person dad. Same scene, two angles. Leo sees something wrong (smell, worried face). Dad knows he burned the eggs and sees Leo's reaction. Showing both sides creates a fuller picture of what happened.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

I am the oldest tree in the park. I have seen this bench built, children grow up, and storms pass. The girl who sits under me every afternoon does not know I am watching. But I am.

Who is the narrator? Is this first-person or third-person? What effect does this narrator choice have on the story?
items.answer: The narrator is the oldest tree, speaking in first-person (uses 'I'). The effect is that we see the park from a long, slow perspective that a human cannot have. The tree has witnessed time passing. This creates a feeling of history, patience, and perhaps loneliness. It also makes the reader see the girl differently, as something small and temporary in the tree's long life.

steps: 'I am the oldest tree' announces the narrator directly. First-person. An object-as-narrator changes perspective completely. The tree sees across time ('I have seen') and from a height. The girl does not know she is being watched. This creates dramatic irony: we know something the character does not. Choosing a tree as narrator shapes what the story can contain and how it feels.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

Maya told her version of the story: 'I was just sitting there, and Sam took the pencil without asking.'

Sam told his version: 'I did not think she was using it. I only borrowed it.'

The story narrator wrote: Sam reached over and took the pencil from Maya's desk while she was looking away.

How many narrators or speakers are there? Whose telling of events do you trust most? Explain.
items.answer: There are three voices: Maya (first-person in her quote), Sam (first-person in his quote), and the third-person narrator. The third-person narrator is usually considered the most neutral and reliable because they describe what happened without having a side. Maya and Sam each have reasons to tell the story in a way that makes them look good.

steps: Maya speaks in first-person. Sam speaks in first-person. The narrator describes the scene in third-person. Maya says she was just sitting there, Sam says he thought she was not using it. Both are self-serving. The narrator describes what was observed: Sam took the pencil while she looked away. Third-person narrators are often more reliable because they do not have a personal stake in how the story is told.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

I do not know how the bird got into our house. My mom screamed. My little sister thought it was funny. My dad opened every window. The bird eventually found the door.

The narrator is first-person, but we learn a lot about other people's reactions. How does first-person narration affect what we know and what we do not know about the other characters?
items.answer: The first-person narrator tells us what they observed: mom screamed, sister laughed, dad opened windows. But we do not know how the narrator felt, only what they saw. We also cannot know the inner thoughts of the other characters because the narrator can only report what they saw and heard, not what others were thinking.

steps: First-person narrators can describe what others do and say, but not what others think. We know the mom screamed (external), the sister laughed (external), the dad opened windows (external). We do not know why the mom screamed or what was in the sister's mind. First-person is powerful for inner feelings but limited for knowing other characters deeply.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

Ben's teacher read a story out loud. The story was about a boy named Jack who said: 'I will climb this mountain, no matter what.'

How many narrators or storytellers are there in total? Name them.
items.answer: There are three levels: the narrator of the text we are reading (third-person, describing the teacher and Ben), the teacher (who is reading aloud), and Jack (who speaks inside the story within the story). Three layers of storytelling.

steps: Layer 1: The text narrator describes the teacher reading to Ben. Third-person. Layer 2: The teacher reads aloud a story (she is a narrator within the story). Layer 3: Inside that story, Jack speaks in first-person. Three storytelling levels, each inside the other.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

Every night I write in my diary. Today I wrote: 'Aisha was mean to me at lunch. She said I was slow. I did not say anything back. I wish I had.'

Who is the narrator of the story overall? Who is the narrator inside the diary? Are they the same person?
items.answer: The narrator of the overall story is a first-person narrator ('Every night I write'). The narrator inside the diary is also a first-person narrator telling about what happened at lunch. Both are the same person at different moments: one narrates the habit of writing, the other narrates a specific event from earlier.

steps: Both are the same 'I.' The outer narration sets the scene (they write in a diary). The inner narration (diary entry) describes a specific event. The author uses two layers of first-person to show the character both in the present (writing) and reflecting on the past (the diary entry). Same narrator, two time frames.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

Zoe and Marco had a fight about who won the race. Then their teacher asked them to each write what happened.

Zoe wrote: 'I crossed the finish line first. I could feel it.'
Marco wrote: 'I touched the line before Zoe. I was there.'

Both use first-person. Why might first-person narration be less reliable when two characters disagree?
items.answer: First-person narration is limited to one person's perspective and feelings. When two people both say 'I' and disagree, neither can be fully objective because they each experienced the event from their own point of view and want to be right. First-person narrators can be honest but still be wrong or incomplete because they only know what they themselves felt and saw.

steps: First-person narrators report their own experience. They may be honest, but honesty is not the same as accuracy. Zoe felt she won. Marco felt he won. Both are first-person accounts. Neither saw the race from above. A third-person narrator or a camera would be more reliable because neither has a personal stake. This is why multiple perspectives matter and why point of view affects the information we get.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

I watched my grandma fold the dumplings. Her hands moved fast and sure. I tried to do it the same way, but mine fell apart. 'It takes time,' she said. 'My grandmother showed me. Now I show you.'

Who is the narrator? What does the grandmother's speech add to the story that the narrator alone could not provide?
items.answer: The narrator is the child, telling their own story in first-person. The grandmother's speech adds her own story: that she was also taught by her grandmother. This creates a chain of teaching across generations. The narrator could only describe what they saw. The grandmother's words reveal the history and meaning behind the skill being passed down.

steps: Narrator: first-person child. Grandmother's speech adds a second layer: 'My grandmother showed me. Now I show you.' The narrator saw the skill being taught. The dialogue reveals the tradition: this has been passed down through generations. Without that line, we would only know the narrator is learning. With it, we understand the full significance of the moment.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

Sam never thought about the janitor, Mr. Ortega, until the day Sam dropped his whole lunch tray. Mr. Ortega came with a mop without being called. When he was done, he said to Sam, 'Happens to the best of us.' Sam never forgot those words.

The narrator is third-person. What would change if Sam were the first-person narrator? What would change if Mr. Ortega were the first-person narrator?
items.answer: If Sam were the narrator: we would know his embarrassment, relief, and feelings in the moment much more directly. If Mr. Ortega were the narrator: we would understand why he said that phrase, perhaps from his own experience of spilling or feeling embarrassed, and we would see Sam from the outside. The third-person narrator shows both without going deep into either.

steps: Third-person can show both characters from the outside without privileging either. Sam as first-person: inner feelings, embarrassment, gratitude. Mr. Ortega as first-person: his history, his reason for the kind words, his view of Sam. The choice of narrator shapes what emotional experience the reader has. Each narrator version would be a different story even though the event is the same.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

I am the moon. Every night I rise and every morning I set. I have watched every child on Earth fall asleep. I am patient. I have all the time in the world.

The narrator is the moon. How does this narrator choice affect the reader's experience of the story?
items.answer: Giving the moon a voice creates a sense of vastness and deep time. The moon is ancient and sees everything from above. Having it speak in first-person makes the reader feel small but also watched and included in something enormous. It creates a feeling of calm, wonder, and belonging.

steps: An object that speaks in first-person is a strong narrative choice. The moon sees all children sleeping, which connects the reader to every other child in the world. 'I have all the time in the world' is both literally true (the moon has existed for billions of years) and emotionally calming. First-person from the moon invites the reader to be seen by something much larger than themselves.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

My father always said: 'Do not be afraid to ask for help.' But I never did ask. The day I finally asked my teacher for help with reading, she smiled and said, 'I wondered when you would come.'

Who are all the voices in this story? How does each voice add something different?
items.answer: Three voices: the narrator ('I never did ask'), the father (quoted memory: 'Do not be afraid to ask for help'), and the teacher ('I wondered when you would come'). Each adds something: the narrator gives inner experience, the father gives wisdom and advice, the teacher's words reveal she had noticed and been waiting. Together they create a complete emotional picture.

steps: Narrator: first-person, inner experience. Father's quote: wisdom from memory, sets up the conflict (the narrator did not follow the advice). Teacher's words: reveal that she already knew, making her seem perceptive and kind. The three voices interact: the father's advice is proven right by the teacher's reaction. The narrator connects all three by telling the story and acting as the bridge.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

Leo read a book where the narrator was a dog. 'If I were telling this story,' Leo thought, 'I would tell it differently.'

With that thought, Leo imagined his own version: 'I live in the best house. My family feeds me and scratches my ears. Life is good.'

In Leo's imagined version, who is the narrator? In the original text, who is the narrator?
items.answer: In the original text, the narrator is a third-person narrator who tells us about Leo. In Leo's imagined version, the narrator is a dog speaking in first-person ('I live,' 'My family,' 'Life is good'). Leo is imagining himself inside the dog's perspective.

steps: Outer text: narrator tells us about Leo in third-person. Leo imagines a first-person dog narrator. Two separate narrative frames. The outer frame has third-person narration. The inner imagined story has first-person narration from the dog's point of view. Leo is essentially writing a first-person story in his head.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

Aisha told the same story three different ways.

Version 1: I was walking to school when I saw a fire truck race past.
Version 2: Aisha was walking to school when a fire truck raced past.
Version 3: We were all walking to school, and then we heard the siren. 'Look!' someone shouted.

What is the point of view in each version? What does each version feel like compared to the others?
items.answer: Version 1: first-person singular (I). Feels personal, immediate, inside one person's experience. Version 2: third-person (Aisha). Feels like an outside observer watching. Version 3: first-person plural (We). Feels communal, shared, like a group experience. Each version creates a different relationship between the reader and the event.

steps: Version 1 is intimate: we are inside the narrator. Version 2 is distant: we watch from outside. Version 3 is communal: the narrator is part of a group, and someone shouts, adding a second voice. Same event, three different experiences for the reader based on narrator choice. Point of view shapes how close or distant the reader feels.

items.prompt:
Read this story below.

Marco grew up and became a teacher. One day, a shy boy in his class reminded him of himself at that age. 'I used to be just like you,' Marco told the boy.

Later that night, Marco wrote in his journal: 'I remember being that boy. I was so quiet. I wanted someone to see me.'

The text narrator is third-person. Marco speaks once and writes in his journal. How do the different voices in this story create a picture of who Marco is?
items.answer: The third-person narrator gives us the facts: Marco is a teacher, he sees himself in the boy, he speaks to the boy. Marco's spoken words tell the boy he was once like him. His journal tells us his inner truth: he was quiet and wanted to be seen. Together the three voices (narrator, Marco speaking, Marco writing) build a complete picture of a man shaped by his own childhood experience.

steps: Narrator: facts and observations. Marco's spoken words: what he chooses to share with the student. Marco's journal: what he thinks privately. The most intimate layer is the journal. Together they show: the present (teacher), the personal connection (recognizing himself), and the deep past (the quiet boy who wanted to be seen). Multiple voices reveal character more fully than any single voice could.
